sources.title: Visuospatial working memory capacity predicts the organization of acquired explicit motor sequences

findings.finding: Working memory is relied on during learning new action sequences for chunking individual action elements together.
findings.quote: they suggest that working memory is relied on during learning new action sequences for chunking individual action elements together.

findings.finding: Individuals naturally group elementary movements into efficient memory units, or chunks, when learning a motor sequence.
findings.quote: human subjects learn a visuomotor sequence by spontaneously chunking the elementary movements, while each chunk acts as a single memory unit.

findings.finding: The striatal system plays a critical role in motor chunking and predictive stimulus-response associations.
findings.quote: The striatal system learns predictive stimulus-response associations and is critical for motor chunking.

principle: When learning a new sequence, breaking movements into smaller clusters or chunks reduces working memory load and improves retention and performance.
for_the_teacher: Break down long movement sequences into smaller groups of three to four elements to match optimal memory chunk sizes.
